Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to conduct hypothesis tests for the difference between two population proportions.

Content:
Suppose we have two populations. Let the proportion of individuals in the first and second populations with a particular characteristic be [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2,] respectively. Independent random samples of size [MATH: n_1] and [MATH: n_2] are drawn from each population.

Content:
Suppose the sample sizes are sufficiently large such that
[MATH: n_i \cdot \widehat{\,p}_i > 5, \qquad n_i\cdot (1-\widehat{\,p}_i)>5, \qquad i=1,2.]
Then, we know that the sampling distributions of our estimates [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2] of [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2] respectively are given by
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1 \sim N\left(p_1, \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}\right), \qquad \widehat{\,p}_2 \sim N\left(p_2, \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right).]

Content:
Since the samples are independent, by the properties of expectation and variance, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E [\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = p_1 - p_2, \qquad \textrm{Var} [\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2] are normally distributed, their difference is also normal, and we have
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2 \sim N\left(p_1 - p_2, \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right).]

Content:
In most practical situations, [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2] are unknown. However, we can approximate the above distribution using estimates obtained from sample data. Thus, we can write

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to conduct hypothesis tests for the difference between two population proportions.

Content:
Suppose we have two populations. Let the proportion of individuals in the first and second populations with a particular characteristic be [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2,] respectively. Independent random samples of size [MATH: n_1] and [MATH: n_2] are drawn from each population.

Content:
Suppose the sample sizes are sufficiently large such that
[MATH: n_i \cdot \widehat{\,p}_i > 5, \qquad n_i\cdot (1-\widehat{\,p}_i)>5, \qquad i=1,2.]
Then, we know that the sampling distributions of our estimates [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2] of [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2] respectively are given by
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1 \sim N\left(p_1, \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}\right), \qquad \widehat{\,p}_2 \sim N\left(p_2, \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right).]

Content:
Since the samples are independent, by the properties of expectation and variance, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E [\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = p_1 - p_2, \qquad \textrm{Var} [\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2] are normally distributed, their difference is also normal, and we have
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2 \sim N\left(p_1 - p_2, \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right).]

Content:
In most practical situations, [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2] are unknown. However, we can approximate the above distribution using estimates obtained from sample data. Thus, we can write

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Pooled vs. Unpooled Estimates of Proportion

Content:
Suppose we wish to carry out the following hypothesis test:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0: p_1 = p_2]
- [MATH: H_1: p_1 > p_2]

Content:
As we just saw, the variance of the difference between the two sampling distributions is

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}.]

Content:
Now, under the null hypothesis, the two proportions are equal. Thus, assuming that [MATH: H_0] is true, we can set

Content:
[MATH: p_1 = p_2 = p]
which gives
[MATH: Var[p^(^)_{1} − p^(^)_{2}]|= (p(1 − p))/(n_{1}) + (p(1 − p))/(n_{2})]

Content:
which simplifies to

Content:
[MATH: Var[p^(^)_{1} − p^(^)_{2}]|= p(1 − p)((1)/(n_{1}) + (1)/(n_{2})).]

Content:
Since the two proportions are equal under the null hypothesis, we can use a pooled estimate [MATH: \overline{p}] of the shared proportion [MATH: p] to form a point estimate.

Content:
[MATH: \overline{p} = \dfrac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2} = \dfrac{n_1\widehat{\,p}_1+n_2\widehat{\,p}_2}{n_1+n_2}]
where [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] give the number of sample elements from the first and second samples, respectively, with the characteristic.

Content:
Thus, our estimate for the variance is
[MATH: \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] =\overline{p}(1-\overline{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right).]
This is similar to the pooled variance estimate we saw in a previous lesson.

Content:
As a result, we can use the following normal approximation:

Content:
